strengths: WorldMirror presents an ambitious and well-executed unification of feed-forward 3D perception tasks, simultaneously handling camera parameters, dense point clouds, depth maps, surface normals, and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) representations within a single feed-forward architecture.

The flexible 'any-prior' prompting mechanism effectively bridges unconstrained reconstruction and prior-guided reconstruction. Representing intrinsics and extrinsics as compact tokens while injecting depth additively into patch tokens enables seamless operation with arbitrary subsets (or complete absence) of priors without architectural changes.

Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments across multiple distinct benchmarks (DTU, 7-Scenes, NRGBD, RealEstate10K, DL3DV, ScanNet, NYUv2) demonstrate consistent state-of-the-art or highly competitive performance against both specialized single-task baselines (e.g., StableNormal, GeoWizard, AnySplat) and generalist models (e.g., VGGT, π³).

The paper is clearly structured and well-illustrated, providing insightful ablation studies on prior embedding representations (single token vs. dense Plücker/raymaps) and novel view synthesis supervision choices.
weaknesses: The core architectural components are largely an integration and extension of existing paradigms (VGGT backbone, DPT heads, AnySplat-style 3DGS heads, and standard token concatenation/addition for conditioning), making the technical novelty primarily system-level rather than foundational.

The paper emphasizes a multi-dimensional curriculum learning strategy (task sequencing, data scheduling, and progressive resolution) as critical for stabilizing multi-task training, but does not provide an ablation study isolating the performance gains or convergence benefits of these curriculum components.

The evaluation of prior prompting assumes clean ground-truth priors (e.g., accurate depth or exact camera poses). There is no analysis evaluating robustness against noisy or imperfect priors (e.g., noisy SLAM poses, sparse/noisy LiDAR depth), which is crucial for real-world deployment.

Detailed runtime, memory footprint, and FLOP analysis across varying view counts and resolutions are missing, leaving the scalability and computational overhead of running all prediction heads simultaneously somewhat unclear.

strengths: Comprehensive and unified formulation: The framework effectively bridges feed-forward multi-view 3D reconstruction and generalizable novel view synthesis, while supporting optional prior prompting (intrinsics, poses, and depth) in a flexible manner.

Extensive experimental validation: The paper evaluates performance across five distinct core tasks (point clouds, camera pose, surface normals, depth, and novel view synthesis) on a wide range of standard benchmarks (e.g., 7-Scenes, DTU, ScanNet, RealEstate10K, DL3DV), showing solid gains over recent baselines such as VGGT, pi3, and AnySplat.

Sound design choices and thorough ablations: The ablation studies justify the design decisions, such as using compact single-token representations for poses and intrinsics over dense Plücker/ray embeddings, as well as the necessity of novel view supervision and loss formulations.

Practical versatility: The model gracefully handles arbitrary subsets of available priors (from none to all) through a simple dynamic dropout injection scheme, demonstrating clear synergistic improvements across tasks when priors are supplied.
weaknesses: Incremental technical novelty at the component level: Many core architecture pieces (e.g., DPT dense prediction heads, alternating attention backbone, standard camera regression) directly follow VGGT, while tokenizing camera parameters and depth has precedent in prior works like Pow3R and UniDepth. The primary innovation is largely system-level integration.

Decoupled training for 3DGS: In the curriculum learning setup (Sec. A.2), the model parameters are frozen when training the 3DGS head. While practically sensible for training stability, this prevents joint gradient feedback from appearance/rendering back into the shared geometric representations, slightly undermining the claim of fully end-to-end multi-task synergy.

Incomplete computational efficiency analysis: Although feed-forward inference time (<2s) is noted in Table 8, a detailed breakdown of memory footprint, throughput, and scaling behavior across varying view counts and image resolutions compared to VGGT and AnySplat is missing.

Mixed performance on dynamic/outdoor domains: The model lags behind pi3 on benchmarks with dynamic objects or autonomous driving scenes (e.g., Sintel in Table 2, KITTI in Table 7), indicating sensitivity to domain shifts and dynamic motion.

strengths: Comprehensive unified framework: The paper successfully integrates multiple fundamental 3D vision tasks—point cloud regression, depth estimation, camera parameter prediction, surface normal estimation, and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)—into a single feed-forward architecture.

Flexible prior prompting mechanism: The multi-modal prompting design accommodates arbitrary subsets of priors (camera intrinsics, camera poses, and depth maps) through specialized tokenization (compact tokens for pose/intrinsics and dense spatial tokens for depth) combined with dynamic random dropping during training.

Strong and extensive empirical results: WorldMirror achieves state-of-the-art or highly competitive performance across a wide range of standard benchmarks (e.g., 7-Scenes, DTU, ScanNet, NYUv2, RealEstate10K, DL3DV), demonstrating improvements over specialized baselines such as VGGT, pi^3, StableNormal, and AnySplat.

Solid experimental validation and ablations: The manuscript includes systematic ablation studies regarding prior embedding techniques (single token vs. dense raymap/Plücker embeddings), multi-task supervisions, and the impact of 3DGS depth gradient consistency.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: The individual architectural and algorithmic components heavily build upon existing frameworks. Specifically, the backbone and core regression heads follow VGGT, the 3DGS prediction closely parallels AnySplat, and the prior injection paradigm reflects ideas from Pow3R and UniDepth. The contribution is primarily system-level integration and scaling.

Evaluation on idealized priors: The experimental evaluation of prior prompting appears to rely exclusively on noise-free ground truth priors. In real-world applications (e.g., LiDAR depth, SLAM poses), priors are inherently noisy, uncalibrated, or sparse. Demonstrating model robustness under noisy, drifted, or partially occluded priors is essential to justify practical utility.

Lack of analysis on multi-task interference and negative transfer: While the paper demonstrates high performance across tasks, it lacks an in-depth ablation comparing the unified multi-task model against single-task equivalents trained under the exact same data regime to analyze potential gradient conflicts or negative transfer among tasks.

High computational requirement and scalability limits: The model requires extensive training resources (32 H20 GPUs across multiple training phases) and, as noted in the limitations, inference memory scales unfavorably when input image counts grow beyond moderate sequences, restricting practical deployment on standard hardware.

strengths: Compelling unified framework: The paper successfully bridges flexible prior conditioning (camera poses, intrinsics, depth) with comprehensive multi-task 3D prediction (point maps, depths, normals, poses, and 3D Gaussians) in an end-to-end feed-forward architecture.

Principled tokenization and fusion design: The distinction between global conditioning (concatenating compact pose and intrinsic tokens) and dense conditioning (element-wise addition of patchified depth tokens) is technically sound and avoids the quadratic computational overhead of token sequence inflation, as supported by ablations in Table 5 and Table 15.

Effective training strategy for conflicting objectives: The decoupled sequential training scheme and the gradient consistency loss between 3DGS rendered depth and predicted pseudo-depth effectively prevent appearance rendering from degrading geometric accuracy.

Extensive and thorough empirical validation: The method is validated across a wide range of benchmarks covering point map reconstruction (7-Scenes, NRGBD, DTU), camera pose estimation (RealEstate10K, TUM-dynamics), surface normal estimation (ScanNet, NYUv2, iBims-1), and novel view synthesis (DL3DV, MatrixCity, VR-NeRF).

Comprehensive ablations and robustness checks: The appendix provides rigorous analyses regarding prior dropout probability, noise sensitivity in prior inputs, inference latency, memory scaling up to hundreds of views, and post-optimization benefits.
weaknesses: Data scale and pretraining confound: The model is initialized from VGGT and further trained on an aggregation of 15 large-scale datasets. While the authors transparently acknowledge this advantage, it makes it challenging to disentangle how much of the performance gain stems from the proposed multi-task synergy versus the expanded training data distribution compared to baselines.

One-directional synergy for appearance: Freezing the geometry backbone when training the 3DGS head mitigates task interference, but it also prevents rendering supervision from refining or backpropagating into the geometric representations, limiting the mutual reinforcement claim specifically for the novel view synthesis branch.

Ambiguity in scene canonicalization under absent pose priors: The pose tokenization relies on normalizing camera translations with respect to the scene centroid and scale factor. It would be beneficial to explicitly clarify how spatial scale and coordinate frames are established when pose priors are completely omitted during inference.

strengths: Comprehensive and ambitious unified framework: The paper successfully unifies heterogeneous 3D vision tasks (sparse-to-dense point clouds, camera poses, multi-view depth maps, surface normal estimation, and 3D Gaussian Splatting) alongside multi-modal prior prompting (camera intrinsics, poses, and depth) into a single transformer-based model.

Extensive empirical evaluation: The method is benchmarked against strong, recent baselines across an unusually broad range of tasks and datasets (e.g., 7-Scenes, NRGBD, DTU for reconstruction; RealEstate10K, Sintel, TUM-dynamics for pose; ScanNet, NYUv2, iBims-1 for normals; DL3DV, RealEstate10K, MatrixCity for novel view synthesis). Performance is consistently competitive or state-of-the-art across all benchmarks.

Thorough and insightful ablation studies: The submission includes comprehensive ablations exploring crucial design choices, such as single-token global prior injection versus dense Plücker/raymap injection (Table 5), addition vs. concatenation for dense depth tokens (Table 15), curriculum/decoupled training vs. joint optimization (Table 13), and robustness against varying degrees of prior noise (Table 12).

Transparency regarding practical usability and computational budget: Appendix F details the wall-clock training time (70 hours on 32 H20 GPUs), per-task GPU memory scaling, maximum supported view counts (up to 1024 views for geometry tasks), and inference latencies.
weaknesses: Incremental architectural novelty: The core model relies heavily on the VGGT architecture, combining its alternating attention backbone and DPT decoders with straightforward token prompting (2-layer MLPs for camera parameters and element-wise addition for patch-embedded depth). While practically effective, the conceptual originality of the architectural modules is modest.

Confounding role of training data scale: The model is initialized from VGGT checkpoints and fine-tuned on an aggregated mixture of 15 diverse 3D datasets. Because many comparison baselines (such as specialized normal estimators or view synthesis frameworks) were trained on significantly less or different data, it is difficult to cleanly disentangle how much performance gain is driven by the unified multi-task formulation versus sheer training data scale and pre-trained backbone quality.

Tension between 'end-to-end unified' claims and decoupled staged training: The paper claims a unified end-to-end framework, yet Section 3.2 and Table 13 indicate that simultaneous end-to-end joint training of appearance (3DGS) and geometry heads leads to noticeable performance degradation. Freezing the geometry backbone to train the Gaussian head separately resolves the issue pragmatically, but weakens the claim of a fully integrated multi-task joint representation.

Loss of absolute metric scale from depth normalization: Normalizing depth maps to [0, 1] preserves relative geometry and improves optimization stability across mixed datasets (Table 16), but discards absolute metric units, which limits utility in downstream robotics applications where calibrated metric depth priors (e.g., from LiDAR) are available.

strengths: Ambitious and unified framework: WorldMirror elegantly unifies flexible multi-modal geometric prior injection (intrinsics, camera poses, dense depth) with comprehensive 3D spatial predictions (point maps, depth maps, camera parameters, surface normals, and 3D Gaussians) within a single feed-forward architecture.

Principled architectural and training design: The tokenization strategy sensibly differentiates global metadata (poses, intrinsics via MLP projection and sequence concatenation) from dense signals (depth maps via additive patch embeddings to avoid quadratic attention blowup, ablated in Tab. 5 & 15). Furthermore, the decoupled sequential curriculum training effectively mitigates optimization conflicts between rendering objectives (3DGS) and metric geometric regression.

Extensive, high-quality empirical evaluation: The paper conducts rigorous evaluations across five distinct tasks and dozens of benchmarks (7-Scenes, NRGBD, DTU, ScanNet, NYUv2, RealEstate10K, DL3DV, MatrixCity, etc.), consistently demonstrating competitive or state-of-the-art results compared to both specialized and generalist baselines.

Thorough analysis and supplementary reporting: The authors provide detailed ablation studies on prior embedding strategies, training strategies, prior dropout sensitivity, robustness to noisy sensor priors, wall-clock training costs, memory usage, and inference latencies across varying view counts.
weaknesses: One-directional synergy between geometry and appearance: Due to the decoupled sequential training where all model parameters are frozen before training the 3DGS head (to prevent rendering objectives from corrupting geometry), the geometry heads do not benefit from multi-view photometric supervision. This partially undermines the broader claim of fully mutual reinforcement between all multi-task objectives.

Confounding impact of pretraining and large-scale training data: The model is initialized from pretrained VGGT weights and trained on an extensive collection of 15 datasets (across 32 H20 GPUs). As acknowledged in Section 5.1, it is difficult to cleanly disentangle how much of the performance advantage over baselines stems from architectural/prior-prompting innovations versus broader dataset scale and compute budget.

Memory bottleneck of the 3DGS prediction head: As reported in Appendix Tab. 17 and 18, while the geometry heads scale up to 1024 views and ~23 GB for 256 views, the 3DGS head consumes over 60.5 GB for 256 views and runs out of memory at 512 views on an H20 GPU, limiting practical deployment for dense capture without chunking.

Absence of noise-aware training: During training, priors are either provided clean or dropped out with probability p=0.5. Although robustness to synthetic noise is evaluated in Appendix D, real-world sensor priors (e.g., noisy mobile SLAM poses or depth sensor drift) are typically imperfect rather than cleanly binary, and the model lacks explicit noise injection during training to learn calibrated uncertainty over imperfect priors.
